newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, under fire, urges campaign finance reform.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, under fire, urges campaign finance reform.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, battered by allegations of improper political fund-raising, on Friday proposed major reform of campaign finance laws including banning money from non-citizens.

"There are many immigrants who play an important role in our country but the essence of our democracy is that the citizens decide. Only citizens can vote. And only citizens' should be able to contribute," Clinton said in remarks prepared for a campaign speech. It aimed to rebuff attacks by Republican presidential nominee Bob Dole, Reform Party candidate Ross Perot and others four days before the Nov. 5 election.

Clinton has been dealing with questions about the White House ties of senior Democratic fundraiser John Huang, who is reported to have raised extensive cash from powerful Asian business interests while also enjoying White House access.

Echoing Dole's call for a ban on donations from non-citizens, Clinton added: "Today it is legal for both parties to receive donations from corporations that are owned by foreign corporations and from individuals who live here legally but are not citizens. The democratic Party has raised money this way: so has the Republican party. In fact much more. It is time to end this practice."

Saying his earlier attempts at campaign finance reform had been thwarted by Dole and the Republicans, Clinton said the time was past for further study of the issue and Congress should swiftly pass reforms.

His specific proposals included outlawing unlimited "soft money" -- or unregulated contributions -- for political parties, restrictions on political action committees that pour money into campaigns and voluntary spending limits for candidates. "It is time to change the rules," he said.
